title.narrative: BLIAP - Being LGBTI in Asia and Pacific, Phase 3, 2020-2021
BLIAP- Att vara HBTQI-person i Asien och Oceanien, Fas 3, 2020-2021

description.narrative: Being LGBTI in Asia and Pacific (BLIAP) is a regional project implemented by UNDP. It has previously been given funding from Sida between 2014-2018. In 2019 the BLIAP entered into a phase 3 with implementation period 2019-2023 and continued to receive Swedish funds for 2019 activities. The Being LGBTI in the Asia Pacific (BLIAP) Phase 3 programme builds upon previous work in Phase 1 and 2. BLIAP Phase 3 (2019-2023) will implement a five-year plan strategically focusing on five development dimensions, set out below. These areas of work build on the recommendations of the Being LGBTI in Asia Regional Dialogue in 2015 and the achievements of BLIA Phase 2. They also reflect the key areas of inclusion identified through a global consultative process with civil society and stakeholders on the LGBTI inclusion index in 2016. The COVID-19 has created a perfect storm of crises across the region, not just in regards to health: COVID-19 creates a socio-economic crise, disproportionately impacting already marginalized persons within societies and causing significant human rights challenges. The pandemic is disrupting the capacity of LGBTI organisations to respond to challenges, and new ways of working need to be developed. According to UNDP, the crisis also presents an opportunity for transformative change and a possibility to build back more inclusively and sustainabily. Sidas assessment is that a cost extension will allow for UNDP to continue to adapt to changing circumstances and support the LGBTI community in times of crises. It is positive that UNDP works with an expanded approach that focuses on adequate representation by young LGBTI-persons and emerging issues such as LGBTI inclusion in climate action and adaptation. This also strengthens the relevance in relation to the on-going Strategy for Regional Asia and the Pacific (2016-2021).

Being LGBTI in Asia and Pacific (BLIAP) är ett regionalt projekt som genomförs av UNDP. Det har tidigare beviljats medel från Sida mellan 2014–2018. År 2019 gick BLIAP in i fas 3 med genomförandeperioden 2019-2023. Fas 3 av Being LGBTI in the Asia Pacific (BLIAP) bygger på tidigare arbete och resultat i fas 1 och 2 och genomförs med fokus på fem strategiska dimensioner. Dessa arbetsområden bygger på rekommendationer från Being LGBTI in Asia Regional Dialogue under 2015 och resultaten från fas 2. De återspeglar också de områden som identifierades som viktigast att inkludera under en global konsultationsprocess med civila samhället och aktörer kring LGBTI inclusion index 2016. UNDP och Sida har haft en nära dialog kring hur COVID-19 och politisk turbulens har påverkat programmet och dess målgrupp. Att vara HBTQI i Asien och Oceanien ökar risken för marginalisering och social exkludering. COVID-19 skapar inte bara en hälsokris, utan även en socio-ekonomisk kris där redan marginaliserade grupper drabbas extra hårt. Samtidigt skapar krisen också en möjlighet att bygga tillbaka bättre på ett sätt som är mer hållbart och inkluderande, och det finns ett momentum att bygga vidare på. Genom en avtalsändring fortsätter ambassaden att stödja UNDP under 2021 som är det sista året för den regionala strategin för Asien och Oceanien. Ambassadens bedömning är att denna avtalsändring möjliggör för UNDP att fortsätta stödja den regionala HBTQI-communityn under en tid av kris. UNDP har arbetat aktivt för att anpassa stödet till den nya situationen och stöd för ökad digital säkerhet kommer också att ingå i budgeten. Strategirelevansen bedöms ha ökat genom att UNDP arbetar mer integrerat med miljö och klimat, genom att verka för ökad representation av HBTQI-personer inom klimatområdet.

UNDP has reported many results from the programme throughout the years both on output and outcome- level, and some of them are highlighted below:
Under objective 1: Increased capacity of LGBTI organizations to mobilize, advocate and contribute to policy dialogue and community empowerment
BLIAP continued to play an important, both direct and contributory, role in building the capacity of civil society organizations in the Asia- Pacific region to address LGBTI issues. This included building capacity of the LGBTI organizations in Asia and Pacific to function more effectively and to advocate and contribute to policy dialogues, as well as creating space to support broadening the diversity of voices in spaces where development agendas are set and issues are prioritized. A small grants programme has been crucial for the BLIAP to reach communities at the grassroots level, especially during COVID pandemic.
Over the years, BLIAP has supported the strengthening of organizational governance, planning, advocacy, and research for multiple regional LGBTI civil society advocacy organizations, most significantly: ASEAN SOGIE Caucus (ASC), the Asia Pacific Transgender Network (APTN), B- change Foundation and Common Language China. The programme has supported capacity assessment and strengthening that enabled the networks to complete legal registration and achieve minimum standards to be eligible as grant recipients. Moreover, BLIAP has supported advocacy efforts and ensured the long-term financial sustainability and effectiveness of the civil society groups. UNDP has also supported the CSOs to successfully strengthen the institutional capacity of ASEAN LGBTI civil society to engage with the United Nations human rights monitoring mechanisms and strengthened organizational governance. APTN and ASC have since positioned themselves in the regional and international arenas as a focal point, amongst their partners, on advocacy for their respective beneficiaries in the region.
- In India, BLIAP supported a national level civil society group, TWEET Foundation and their project Project Samarthan, to empower the transmen community in India to participate in advocacy dialogues and to build regional community support systems. The activities supported included capacity building workshops on legal awareness, leadership training and community mobilization. This small grants programme was an opportunity to bolster the capacity of transmen-led civil society group and create a new transgender network at the national level. As a direct result of Project Samarthan, two transmen grassroots organizations are in the process of registering their organizations and have been equipped with the expertise needed to become fully fledged and sustainable organization.
- In the Pacific BLIAP has been committed to reaching communities often left behind when it comes to regional activities, interventions and policy dialogues. To this end, UNDP were able to support Pride Cook Islands, and help them to establish their organization and work on LGBTI rights at the national level. The project Tikaanga aiteite e tiratiratu ei te oraanga ote iti tangata Kuki Airani katoatoa strengthened the digital capacities of the LGBTI community (especially young LGBTI persons) and enhanced the organizations digital presence when it came to educational and awareness programmes, and services to assist individuals with domestic and mental health issues.
- In the Philippines, the small grants programme supported the efforts of national level civil society group, San Julian Pride (SJP), in LGBTQI-Inclusive Disaster Risk Reduction and Management (DRRM) in the Municipality San Julian, Eastern Samar, Philippines. The objectives of the project were to build San Julian Prides capability to influence local DRRM in the municipality of San Julian, Eastern Samar, Philippines toward applying a SOGIESC/ intersectional lens for DRRM and to alleviate the effects of the COVID-19 crisis on the LGBTQI population of San Julian, Eastern Samar, Philippines. This grant marked the first time that a local civil society organization would be initiating a DRRM project and in doing so, set a precedent for CSOs in participatory governance in the context of climate change and DRRM. Most significantly, SJP was able to engage the Local Disaster Risk Reduction Management Councils (LDRRMC) in a training on SOGIE in DRR.
- In Lao PDR, BLIAP supported the Proud to Be Us Laos, a local grassroots organisation, to support their ongoing work on Diversity & Inclusion in the workplace, and work closely with businesses to translate the global UN Standards of Conduct into local action. This partnership builds on the 2021 Study and Manual on Diversity and Inclusion in the Workplace undertaken by Proud to Be Us Laos and the Faculty of Law and Political Science of the National University of Laos and aims to contribute to the national dialogue on ending discrimination faced by LGBTI people, and the business case in ensuring that LGBTI people have equal opportunities in employment and enjoy a safe, inclusive and empowering working environment.
- In Thailand, UNDP Thailand engaged with the transgender community and other LGBTI minority groups who were left furthest behind by COVID-19. Examples of interventions including partnering with grassroots organizations, such as Sisters Pattaya, to organize trainings on how to do make-up and how to utilize this to make a living for transgender women in Pattaya, some of which were working in the entertainment industry and others who worked as sex workers. There has been increased demand from civil society groups to continue to provide hands on training to the marginalized community in order to ensure that they can receive an income as most are not able to access government schemes.
- In Vietnam, UNDP has been working closely with civil society groups on the legal and policy environment and supported C4TRANS - a coalition of civil society organizations working for transgenders right in Vietnam. Organisations within the coaliton are working together to ensure that policymakers are aware of transgender communitys opinion on the contents presented in the draft Gender Affirmation Law and that the concerns and voices of transgender community and international experts reach the Ministry of Health and open up entry point for future advocacy efforts. UNDP Viet Nam also supported the 3rd National LGBTI Summit, bringing together over 170 LGBTIQ leaders, activists, their parents and allies, Embassies, UN agencies, NGOs, private sectors, healthcare providers, psychologists, and government agencies across Vietnam. Many underrepresented groups within the LGBTIQ community showed up and spoke out at the Summit 2021, including LGBTIQ people with disabilities, ethnic minorities LGBTIQ, LGBTIQ living with HIV, LGBTIQ children, and adolescents, etc. More importantly, for the first time at the Stronger Together Summit, representatives and allies of three underserved groups, LGBTIQ youth, transgender persons, and LBQ women, made official announcements and discussed specific action plans towards Rights and Health for all. Summit 2021 has provided the impetus for many initiatives including Working group for LGBTIQ Children and Adolescent, LGBTIQ Advocacy Coalition, LGBTIQ-led Social Innovation and Impact business Lab (Rainbow SIB Lab), Working Group on Sexual and gender-based violence, working group to improve the quality of health services and end HIV/AIDS.
- In China, the programme was able to provide support to increase the capacity and participation of LGBTI community groups in dialogue and advocacy with governments (including policymakers and legislators), and other sectors including private sector, education, health, media, and youth development partners on the development, implementation and monitoring of LGBTI inclusive and protective laws, policies and practices and promotion of equitable access to opportunities and services that meet the needs of LGBTI people. UNDP China supported both online and offline training workshops organized by Beijing LGBT Center to train mental health professionals, including psychological counselors, psychology teachers, medical students, social workers, and professionals who work on sexuality and gender related issues. Twenty mental health professionals participated in the off-line workshops, and nearly 300 people participated in the online training.
Under Objective 2: Through community mobilization and advocacy (with law makers, local governments, judiciary, and NHRIs), to ensure the development and enforcement of protective laws and policies (including anti-violence/anti-discrimination laws and policies)
- BLIAP has played an important role in influencing policy and laws, through evidence generation and direct capacity building support to government departments and policymakers; and by bringing its strategic advantage and approach into partnerships with civil society and other types of organizations that have similar, or overlapping, objectives. Often through requests from national governments, the programme has contributed to the development of 24 supportive laws and policies (in various legislative stages) across eight countries, supporting and improving the gender-responsiveness of legal systems, legal gender recognition, anti-discrimination, and civil partnerships. For example; support to the passing of the Transgender Persons Protection of Rights Act in Pakistan, the support to the drafting of the Civil Partnership Registration law in Thailand, the Transgender Bill in India, the Gender Recognition Law in China (Hong Kong SAR), the Citizenship Bill in Nepal, and more.
- BLIAP also continued its work with Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity, Expression and Sex Characteristic (SOGIESC) rights with National Human Rights Institutions (NHRIs) in the region. For example, during the third phase, the programme developed an e-course on SOGIESC issues for NHRI staff and developed a resources for NHRIs showcasing studies of good practice in response to the impact of COVID-19 on LGBTI communities. These interventions strengthened the capacity of NHRIs to promote and protect human rights in relation to SOGIESC, whilst also serving as an opportunity for NHRIs to exchange experiences, understand and respond to the vulnerabilities of LGBTI communities. NHRIs engaged included those of Australia, Fiji, Bangladesh, India, Mongolia, Myanmar, Nepal, New Zealand, Philippines, Sri Lanka, Thailand, and Timor-Leste. The partnership between UNDP/Asia-Pacific Forum and the NHRIs under the BLIAP was also directly referred to in a joint statement made by the NHRIS on 18th of June 2019. The statement recognized the unique role that NHRIs play to facilitate the integration of international human rights principles into domestic legislation, and to coordinate with governments and civil society to foster an environment of collaboration and cooperation and explicitly pledged continued support to promote freedom from violence and discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics in accordance with the mandates of the NHRIs.
- In terms of laws and policies, the Civil Code of China came into effect on January 1st, 2021. As the first civil code in the legal history of China and the fundamental civil law of China, the Civil Code is relevant to every one's daily life, including LGBTI people and PLHIV. BLIAP engaged a legal expert from the project Expert Advisory Group to conduct an analysis of the impact of the newly adopted Civil Code to demonstrate the effect of the new Civil Code on LGBTI people in China. It analyzed the gaps of the current law, identify best practice cases in judicial practice, and provided policy recommendations for future legal advocacy.
- In Thailand, UNDP has signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the Department of Rights and Liberties Protection (DRLP) of the Ministry of Justice (MOJ) to support the joint implementation of activities to strengthen SOGI-responsiveness in the Thai justice system. Building on a national situation assessment of the management of transgender inmates in prisons, and the first ever national workshop on SOGIE in closed settings (2018), UNDP in partnership with the MOJ supported the mapping of international good practices for the management of transgender people in prisons, released in 2020. Based on the findings and recommendations, a standard operating procedure (SOP) was developed for consideration of the Department of Corrections (DOC) to improve the management of transgender prisoners in Thailand.The SOP addresses some of the main findings of the 2018 assessment, such as evidence that lack of legal gender recognition in Thailand leads to an absence of specific regulations to support the management of transgender inmates, including for crucial health and safety needs. It is expected that the DOC will adopt or adapt the SOP in their practice in the management of transgender prisoners in the Thai justice system. Recognizing the value of this work, the DOC has also expressed interest in co-convening with UNDP an ASEAN-level meeting to discuss shared challenges of transgender prisoners in closed settings, findings of the research, and the possibility of developing additional international guidance similar to considerations for women prisoners encapsulated in the Bangkok Rules.
- In India, UNDP supported NACO with the development of new national guidelines on Stigma and Discrimination related to HIV, which are currently under review by the Government. UNDP also supported wide-ranging consultations on the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Rules 2020. As a result, MoSJE took on board most of the recommendations in the final rules. UNDP has supported the development of a framework document on the Welfare measures of the Transgender community as envisaged under the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2019 and Rules 2020.
Under Objective 3: Through community mobilization and engagement with key stakeholders (such as religious organizations, the private sector, law enforcement authorities, educational institutions), address stigma and discrimination and end harmful practices that fuel human rights violations against LGBTI individuals in public and private settings, and to ensure LGBTI individuals have equal access to public services.
- UNDP in Thailand is actively working with private sector companies to support a more efficient and equitable workplace and contributes to the advancement of gender equality and the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals. The long-term engagement and collaboration with Sansiri, one of the largest real estate developers in Thailand led to Sansiri becoming the first Thai company to sign up to the global Standards of Conduct. UNDP in Thailand also supported Siam commercial Bank and Sansiri to provide equal opportunities for same-sex couples looking to co-borrow for a joint home.
- In 2021, UNDP China supported Beijing LGBT Center to conduct the first national research on LGBT workplace inclusion in the private sector. The research has produced a report with important data, best practices, and policy advice. This research has provided critical data that demonstrate the current situation of workplace discrimination based on SOGIESC, and also evidence for potential social and economic benefits (the business case) of workplace LGBT inclusion in China.
- BLIAP has also contributed to the creation of a UNDP regional youth project on Leadership, Innovation and Entrepreneurship (Youth Co:Lab) initiative, which focuses on youth entrepreneurship and 21st century skill building. The collaboration provide LGBTI youth with the opportunity to engage with the social enterprise ecosystem and translate their ideas into business solutions that are not only instrumental to their personal growth, but also of benefit to the wider LGBTI community. The Youth Co:Lab work triggered the development of a first- of -its- kind initiative in India: Innovations Marketplace for Gender Equality (IMGE), in amidst the Covid pandemic. It focused exclusively on solutions related to Gender Based Violence (GBV) and increasing livelihood opportunities for young LGBTI persons. Led by Youth Co:Lab India and Being LGBTI in Asia and the Pacific, in collaboration with Atal Innovation Mission (NITI Aayog) the initiative was facilitated and organised by LGBTI practitioners and mentors. It became an interactive platform for youth LGBTI persons to develop and launch their innovative solutions for issues encountered by their communities. It was clear that there is a real demand for these kinds of platforms over 100 LGBTI youth innovators applied, of which 20 unique entrepreneurs, social innovators and youth leaders were selected to join the three-month intensive mentorship and incubation programme.
- In 2022, UNDP together with UNESCO launched an e-course which provides training for digital security and protection for LGBTI Youth. The training modules includes digital security risks online, how to navigate online spaces effectively and safely, mental health and cyber- bullying and misinformation online/trusted sources online. The collaboration with UNESCO was part of the initiative: Building a safe and inclusive education sector which carries out regional activities that support implementation of joint work on SOGIE issues in Asia and the Pacific. The project made significant progress in addressing SOGIE-based bullying in education settings through partnership with UNESCO.
When it comes to data generation, research findings produced by the programme are being actively used in advocacy, policymaking, and capacity building. Although direct attribution is difficult to assign to any single actor in complex reform processes, the programme can trace contributions from research into legal and policy reform at least in China, India, Pakistan, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam. BLIAP has completed six multi-country research initiatives on LGBTI inclusion covering 19 countries as well as national level studies. For example, BLIAPs research work on legal gender recognition, which included Pakistan, contributed to the debates culminating in the passing of the Transgender (Protection of Rights) Bill in 2018. Subsequent to the passing of the Bill, and following participation of the Punjab social protection authority at the legal gender recognition multi-country round- table, BLIAP has been called to provide technical assistance to the drafting of state-level transgender welfare policies in Punjab. This will help to operationalize some of the provisions of the Bill.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
